title: Reformed deny faith as disposing/formal cause of forensic absolution
source_text: LIV. Cum autem Reformati distinguant justificationem a sanctificatione, & per justificari non aliud intelligant, quam in judicio divino absolvi, quando negant fidem nos justificare per modum dispositionis, aut per modum formae, id est, ut justitiam, seu partem justitiae per quam justificamur, mens eorum est, fidem non esse talem dispositionem, quae remissionem peccatorum nostrorum mereatur, vel efficiat: & etiam fidei, vel actum, vel habitum, non esse partem justitiae illius, propter quam, & cujus merito a reatu peccatorum nostrorum absolvimur, quae est sola Christi obedientia; licet sit conditio sine qua istam absolutionem consequi non possumus: quod non pugnat cum doctrina Ecclesiae Romanae.
pass_a_gloss: But when the Reformed distinguish justification from sanctification, and by being justified understand nothing else than to be absolved in the divine judgment, when they deny that faith justifies us by way of disposition or by way of form—that is, as the righteousness or part of the righteousness by which we are justified—their mind is that faith is not such a disposition as merits or effects the remission of our sins; and also that neither the act nor the habit of faith is a part of that righteousness on account of which and by whose merit we are absolved from the guilt of our sins, which is the obedience of Christ alone; although it is a condition without which we cannot obtain that absolution: which does not conflict with the doctrine of the Roman Church.
pass_b_english: Reformed: justify = forensic absolution; faith neither merits nor is the righteousness that absolves—Christ's obedience alone is.
Faith is the necessary condition; this need not clash with Rome once senses are sorted.

lemmas.gloss: to be absolved in the divine judgment

choices.why: Faith required, not meritorious/formal cause of forensic justitia.
